hazards.bare-face-check: You leaned in over the open cleaner to look — no goggles. A splash off a moving line or a bucket doesn't wait for you to notice it's coming, and the label on a caustic or acid line cleaner says eye protection for exactly this reason, not as a formality before the real work starts.
hazards.mixing-chemicals: That's an acid-based cleaner sitting open next to the caustic bucket already in use. Acid and caustic line cleaners meeting each other, whether in a drain or a bucket, react hard enough to throw a corrosive splash and a cloud of gas — the SDS for each one exists specifically so they never share a container or a moment.
hazards.unlabeled-bottle: The line cleaner's been decanted into a spray bottle with no label on it. Cal/OSHA's hazard communication rule follows the chemical, not the original container — an unlabeled bottle of caustic under the bar is a bottle nobody after you will know to treat with any caution at all.
hazards.untagged-handle: This tap handle never got tagged with the others. A line mid-clean that isn't tagged looks exactly like a line that's ready to pour, and the only thing standing between a customer and a glass of line cleaner is whether every handle got marked, not just most of them.

interrupts.alert: A customer orders an IPA off the tagged tap, and a colleague reaches for the handle to pour it.
interrupts.cue: Stop them — that handle's tagged for a reason, not out of service by accident.
interrupts.missNote: The colleague poured off the tagged IPA tap while it was still running cleaning solution. A tag that gets overridden the first time someone's in a hurry isn't protecting anybody.
interrupts.why: A tag only protects a customer if it actually stops the next person who reaches for that handle; the line behind it is mid-clean and running cleaning solution right now, and the fastest way to make sure nobody pours from it is pointing at exactly what's already marked on it.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the tag on the handle, not the pump you're holding. Point at what already says not to pour from it.

interrupts.alert: The open cleaner bottle gets knocked over on the bar top behind you.
interrupts.cue: Get to the spill kit — don't just wipe it with a bar rag.
interrupts.missNote: The spill got wiped up with a bar rag instead of the spill kit. Spreading a corrosive thinner across the bar top, and onto the rag itself, is worse than the spill it started as.
interrupts.why: A corrosive spill on a bar top isn't a bar-rag job — a rag spreads it thinner across a bigger surface and puts it on whoever's hand touches that rag next; the spill kit's neutraliser and absorbent are the only correct first move.
interrupts.wrongNote: It's the spill kit. A bar rag doesn't neutralise anything — it just moves the chemical somewhere else.

lateNotes.cleaner-pump: The lines get tagged and the keg disconnected before any cleaner goes anywhere near them.
lateNotes.contact-timer: Contact time starts once the solution is actually in the line, not before it's pumped through.
lateNotes.keg-reconnect: Kegs go back on once the line reads a neutral pH, not before.
lateNotes.ph-strip: The pH gets tested after the flush, not before — there's nothing but cleaner in the line until then.

name: Draught Line Cleaning

passRule.note: stars >= 2 and no unsafe action (WebXR/shared/records.js passed())

steps.cue: Check the drum label, then pull the matching safety data sheet.

itemNotes.cleaner-label: Caustic or acid — today's drum is labelled, and the label decides which neutraliser and which PPE apply for the rest of this clean.
itemNotes.sds-sheet: The safety data sheet for whichever chemical is loaded — first aid, ventilation and spill response all live here, and Cal/OSHA's hazard communication rule expects it read, not just stocked on a shelf.

steps.prompt: Check the drum label, then pull the matching safety data sheet.
steps.title: Identify the cleaner and its SDS
steps.why: A bar alternates between caustic and acid line cleaners depending on what's building up in the lines, and the two are handled differently enough — different PPE, different first aid, never mixed with each other — that the whole clean starts with confirming which one is actually in the bucket today.

steps.cue: Both on before the cleaner comes off the shelf.
steps.prompt: Both on before the cleaner comes off the shelf.
steps.title: Goggles and gloves before the bottle opens
steps.why: Caustic and acid line cleaners are both corrosive to skin and eyes at working strength, and a splash happens at the moment you're least braced for it — opening the container, not partway through pumping — which is why the PPE goes on first, not after the first splash proves it was needed.

steps.cue: Set the spill kit where you can reach it before you start pumping.
steps.prompt: Set the spill kit where you can reach it before you start pumping.
steps.title: Stage the spill kit
steps.why: A corrosive spill on a bar top full of glassware and electrical outlets is not something you want to be locating supplies for after it happens — staging the kit first is what makes the response take ten seconds instead of two minutes.

steps.cue: Tag all three handles on this line before any cleaner goes in.
steps.prompt: Tag all three handles on this line before any cleaner goes in.
steps.title: Tag every affected tap "Do Not Pour"
steps.why: A customer at the rail and a colleague working the well both read a tap handle the same way — available unless it says otherwise. Every handle on the line being cleaned gets its own tag, because the one left untagged is the one somebody pours from.

steps.cue: Uncouple the keg and swap the line onto the cleaning pump.
steps.prompt: Uncouple the keg and swap the line onto the cleaning pump.
steps.title: Disconnect the keg for the cleaning loop
steps.why: Cleaning solution runs a closed loop through the line and back to the bucket, not into a keg of beer — the coupler comes off and the pump goes on before any solution moves.

steps.cue: Hold the pump running until solution has moved all the way through the line.
steps.holdBreakNote: You stopped before the solution reached the far end. Restart the pump — a half-filled line hasn't been cleaned, it's been half cleaned.
steps.prompt: Hold the pump running until solution has moved all the way through the line.
steps.title: Pump the cleaning solution through
steps.why: A partial pump leaves clean beer in one stretch of tubing and cleaner in the next, and neither half gets what it needs — the whole line has to see the solution before contact time means anything.

steps.cue: Let the solution sit in the line for the full contact time on the label.
steps.holdBreakNote: You flushed before the contact time finished. The solution needs the full time on the label to actually break down what's built up in the line — start the hold again.
steps.prompt: Let the solution sit in the line for the full contact time on the label.
steps.title: Hold contact time
steps.why: The chemical does its work by sitting against the beer-stone and yeast film built up on the inside of the tubing, not by passing through it — cutting the contact time short is the single most common reason a line that was 'just cleaned' still tastes off a week later.

steps.cue: Hold the flush valve at a steady rate until the line runs clear.
steps.holdBreakNote: The flush rate drifted out of band. Too slow leaves cleaner sitting in the line, too hard risks a fitting — bring it back to a steady flow.
steps.prompt: Hold the flush valve at a steady rate until the line runs clear.
steps.title: Flush the line with water
steps.why: Too slow a flush leaves cleaner sitting in the low points of the line; too hard a flush can push water back past a fitting that isn't rated for it — a steady, held-open flow is what actually clears the tubing end to end.

steps.cue: Dip the strip at the tap and commit while it reads neutral.

gauge.label: pH
gauge.missNote: Not neutral yet — keep flushing and test again before this line goes anywhere near a keg.

steps.prompt: Dip the strip at the tap and commit while it reads neutral.
steps.title: Test the line with pH paper
steps.why: A line that still reads acidic or basic still has cleaning chemical in it no matter how much water has gone through — the strip is the only honest answer to 'is it out yet,' and neutral is the only reading that means yes.

steps.cue: Couple the keg back onto the now-neutral line.
steps.prompt: Couple the keg back onto the now-neutral line.
steps.title: Reconnect the kegs
steps.why: The line only goes back into beer service once the pH test has confirmed there's nothing left in it to confirm against — reconnecting on a hunch instead of a reading is exactly the shortcut this whole procedure exists to remove.

steps.cue: Pour and dump the first glass off each tap, then pull the "Do Not Pour" tags.
steps.prompt: Pour and dump the first glass off each tap, then pull the "Do Not Pour" tags.
steps.title: Discard the first pour and clear the tags
steps.why: The first pour off a freshly cleaned line still carries trace cleaner and the standing water from the flush — it gets poured out, not into a glass someone's paying for, and the tags come off only once there's a clean pour behind them to prove it.

steps.cue: Record the date, the chemical, the contact time and the final pH.
steps.prompt: Record the date, the chemical, the contact time and the final pH.
steps.title: Log the clean
steps.why: The cleaning log is what turns 'we did this' into something a health inspector, the next shift or the brewery's own quality rep can actually check against a schedule instead of taking on faith.

tagline: Beer lines cleaned to the SDS: goggles and gloves, taps tagged, solution pumped and given its contact time, flushed to a neutral pH, kegs back on and the first pour thrown away
